prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: USAspending.gov
Description: USAspending.gov is the official source for spending data for the U.S. Government. Its mission is to show the American public what the federal government spends every year and how it spends the money. You can follow the money from the Congressional appropriations to the federal agencies and down to local communities and businesses.
URL: https://usaspending.gov/

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: USAspending.gov
Description: USAspending.gov is the official source for spending data for the U.S. Government. Its mission is to show the American public what the federal government spends every year and how it spends the money. You can follow the money from the Congressional appropriations to the federal agencies and down to local communities and businesses.
URL: https://usaspending.gov/

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research USAspending.gov comprehensively, covering its publisher, legal authority, history, data characteristics, users, and public benefits.I have a good foundation. Let me dig deeper into the data model, access methods, data quality issues, and users.Let me gather more on data licensing, entity identifiers, and who actually uses the data.Search limit reached, but I have comprehensive material from the site's own documentation, Treasury's Financial Manual, GAO reports, CRS, and primary statutes. Here is the complete report.

---

# USAspending.gov: A Comprehensive Dataset Report

**Verification note:** The title and description you provided are accurate — they match, nearly verbatim, the official "About" language on the site. One nuance worth knowing: USAspending.gov is technically a *platform/website plus API* that publishes an evolving family of datasets (award data, account-level budget data, subaward data), rather than a single static dataset.

---

## 1. What It Is

USAspending.gov is the **official source for spending data of the U.S. Federal Government**. It lets the public trace money from **Congressional appropriations → federal agency accounts → individual awards (contracts, grants, loans, etc.) → recipients, down to local communities and businesses**. It covers:

- **Award data** (prime awards and subawards): contracts, contract IDVs (indefinite delivery vehicles), grants, direct payments, loans, insurance, and other financial assistance — transaction-level detail back to **FY 2001** (via bulk download; Advanced Search begins FY 2008).
- **Account-level data**: budget authority, obligations by program activity, object class, and federal account, reported monthly by 100+ agencies.
- **Recipient data**: names, locations, unique identifiers (UEI; formerly DUNS), parent entities.
- **Special lenses**: COVID-19 and disaster/emergency spending profile pages.

Source: [usaspending.gov/about](https://www.usaspending.gov/about), [Data Sources PDF](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/data-sources-download.pdf)

---

## 2. Publisher and Governance

- **Current publisher:** U.S. Department of the Treasury, **Bureau of the Fiscal Service** (Data Transparency team). Responsibility was **transferred from OMB to Treasury by the DATA Act of 2014**.
- **OMB's continuing role:** OMB co-develops the government-wide data standards and issues implementation memoranda (e.g., M-17-04 on DATA Act reporting; M-22-02 on new financial assistance transparency reporting requirements).
- **Data providers:** 100+ federal agencies submit standardized files monthly (quarterly was the original cadence; **all agencies moved to monthly reporting starting FY 2022**). Each agency has a designated **Senior Accountable Official (SAO)** who certifies submissions.
- **Authoritative upstream sources:** FPDS-NG (contracts), SAM.gov, the GTAS (Governmentwide Treasury Account Symbol) system, and agencies' own financial systems. USAspending ingests, validates (via the **DATA Act Broker**), and republishes these data.
- **Software:** The platform is built on open-source code (see [github.com/fedspendingtransparency](https://github.com/fedspendingtransparency)) using Agile, user-centered development.

Source: [Treasury Financial Manual, TFM Volume I Part 2 Chapter 6000](https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov), [CRS Report R44027](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44027)

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandates

| Authority | What it requires |
|---|---|
| **FFATA of 2006** (P.L. 109-282, 31 U.S.C. § 6101 note) | A single, free, public, searchable website disclosing all federal awards over **$25,000** (grants, contracts, loans, other financial assistance), including recipient name, amount, transaction type, agency, location, and unique identifiers. Co-sponsored by Sens. Coburn, Obama, McCain, and Carper. |
| **Government Funding Transparency Act of 2008** | Amended FFATA to require prime recipients to report **first-tier subaward** details (effective for awards from Oct. 1, 2010). |
| **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009** (P.L. 111-5) | Stimulus reporting that fed into USAspending. |
| **DATA Act of 2014** (P.L. 113-101) | The big one: expanded FFATA to disclose **direct agency expenditures** and **link awards to programs and appropriations**; established **government-wide data standards**; transferred the site to Treasury; simplified reporting to reduce compliance costs; and required agency accountability for data quality. |
| **Congressional Budget Justification Transparency Act of 2021** | Required agencies to publish their congressional budget justifications and link budget materials to spending data. |
| **Implementing policy:** 2 CFR §§ 25, 170, 200; OMB Circular A-11; OMB memoranda (Open Government Directive 2010, M-17-04, MPM 2016-03, M-22-02) | Operational reporting rules, UEI registration, subaward and executive-compensation reporting. |

Per Treasury's Financial Manual, the **primary statutory authority is FFATA, as amended by the DATA Act and the CBTA of 2021**.

Sources: [Public Law 109-282 text](https://www.congress.gov/109/statute/STATUTE-120/STATUTE-120-Pg1186.pdf), [usaspending.gov/about](https://www.usaspending.gov/about), [TFM Ch. 6000](https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov)

---

## 4. History and Timeline

- **Sept. 26, 2006** — President Bush signs FFATA; it required the website by January 1, 2008.
- **Dec. 13, 2007** — **OMB launches USAspending.gov**, ahead of the statutory deadline, pulling from FPDS and FAADS. It replaced over 30 years of Census Bureau reports (Federal Aid to States; Consolidated Federal Funds Report).
- **2008–2010** — Subaward reporting added (via the FFATA Subaward Reporting System, FSRS).
- **May 9, 2014** — DATA Act signed.
- **April 2016** — Treasury publishes the **DATA Act Information Model Schema (DAIMS)**, the first government-wide spending data standard.
- **May 2017** — First DATA Act-standard agency submissions (File A/B/C reporting); "Beta.USAspending.gov" runs in parallel.
- **2017–2018** — Treasury's rebuilt USAspending.gov becomes the sole site; GAO's early reviews find severe award-data accuracy problems (see §6).
- **FY 2017 Q2 onward** — Agency Submission Statistics page tracks completeness.
- **FY 2022 (Oct. 2021)** — All agencies shift to **monthly** reporting.
- **April 4, 2022** — Federal government retires **DUNS numbers**; recipients identified by the **Unique Entity Identifier (UEI)** issued through SAM.gov. (Historical DUNS fields persist in older records.)
- **Nov. 2023** — DAIMS rebranded/expanded as the **Governmentwide Spending Data Model (GSDM)** to reflect post-DATA Act legislation.
- **Ongoing** — COVID-19 and disaster/emergency spending tracking; iterative Agile releases many times per year.

Sources: [OMB launch press release, Dec. 13, 2007](https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/omb/pubpress/2007/121307_usaspending.html), [CRS R44027](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44027), [TFM Ch. 6000](https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov), [usaspending.gov "Story of Spending Transparency"](https://www.usaspending.gov/featured-content/data-you-can-trust/the-story-of-spending-transparency)

---

## 5. Data Model and Content

- **Standard:** The **GSDM** (formerly DAIMS) defines every element, relationship, and source. Data is submitted as lettered files (File A: appropriations account balances; B: obligations by object class/program activity; C: award-level obligations; D1/D2: award data; E: subawards and executive compensation).
- **Key identifiers (critical for preservation/linkage):**
  - **FAIN** (Federal Award Identification Number) — financial assistance awards
  - **PIID** (Procurement Instrument Identification Number) — contracts
  - **URI** (Unique Record Identifier) — other awards
  - **UEI** (and legacy DUNS) — recipients
  - **TAS** (Treasury Account Symbol) — links awards to federal accounts
- **Time semantics:** Federal fiscal year runs **Oct. 1–Sept. 30**. Obligations ≠ outlays (an obligation is a binding agreement; outlays follow later).
- **Excluded data:** classified/national-security information, PII (individuals' awards are aggregated or redacted, e.g., Social Security recipients appear under aggregate pseudo-recipient entries), proprietary source data, and direct payments to individuals like Economic Impact Payments.

Sources: [Data Sources PDF](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/data-sources-download.pdf), [Analyst's Guide to Federal Spending Data](https://www.usaspending.gov/federal-spending-guide), [About the Data PDF](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/about-the-data-download.pdf)

---

## 6. Data Quality — What Every User Must Know

GAO has audited the site repeatedly; the trajectory is improving but caveats persist:

- **GAO-18-138 (2017):** Only **0–1% of award records** were fully consistent with agency sources (56–75% for budgetary records).
- **GAO-20-75 (FY2018 Q4):** Award-record full consistency improved to **24–34%**; budgetary records to **84–96%**. Eleven agencies failed to submit that quarter.
- **GAO-22-104702 (2021):** Website display largely consistent with certified data, but 19 of 101 agencies omitted the File C budget-award linkage; **hundreds of billions in obligations reported with program activity "Unknown/Other."**
- **GAO-24-106237 (2024):** Subaward data problems persist — **~26% of non-COVID and ~11% of COVID grant subawards are likely duplicates**; missing fields and impossibly large amounts found. COVID-19 known adjustments totaled ~$140B through June 2023 (GAO-24-106214).
- **Standing caveats:** (a) **DoD procurement data has a ~90-day delay**; (b) inconsistent application of *Award Description* and *Place of Performance* standards across agencies; (c) **reporting requirements and standards have changed over time** — older fiscal years (pre-DATA Act, especially pre-FY2008) are markedly less reliable; (d) agencies periodically republish/recertify prior periods, so data can be **retroactively restated**.

The site's own guidance is candid: *"higher quality data are generally found in more recent fiscal years."*

Sources: [GAO-18-138](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-18-138), [GAO-20-75](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-20-75), [GAO-22-104702](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-104702), [GAO-24-106237](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-24-106237.pdf)

---

## 7. Access Channels (for data librarians, scientists, and preservationists)

1. **Interactive site** — Advanced Search, Award/Agency/Recipient/Location profiles, COVID-19 and disaster spending pages.
2. **Award Data Archive** — pre-built, instant FY-by-FY national files: `Contracts_Full` / `Contracts_Delta`, `Assistance_Full` / `Assistance_Delta` (deltas let you reconstruct updates to previously published data).
3. **Custom Award Data / Custom Account Data downloads** — on-demand filtered CSVs/TSVs, the only web route to pre-FY2008 data (back to FY2001).
4. **REST API** — [api.usaspending.gov](https://api.usaspending.gov), documented endpoints, bulk-download endpoints (`/api/v2/bulk_download/awards/`, `list_monthly_files/`), disaster-spending endpoints; free, no key required.
5. **Full PostgreSQL database snapshots** — downloadable archives of the entire database, **over 1.5 TB** and growing; restore takes hours. Intended for advanced users.
6. **Open-source codebase** on GitHub (fedspendingtransparency organization), enabling reproducibility of the ETL pipeline.
7. **Documentation set** — Data Sources & Methodology, Data Dictionary, "About the Data," the **Analyst's Guide to Federal Spending Data** (an excellent citable reference, with a suggested citation format), training videos, and versioned GSDM releases.

---

## 8. Licensing and Intellectual Property

- Data on the site is **open and freely reusable** — Treasury explicitly permits copying, adapting, and redistributing for **commercial and non-commercial** purposes.
- **One important carve-out:** a **Limitation on Permissible Use of Dun & Bradstreet (D&B) Data** applies to DUNS numbers and associated business information, mostly in records predating the April 4, 2022 DUNS-to-UEI transition. D&B "Open Data" elements may be used with attribution but not as a bulk substitute for D&B's commercial products; other D&B data may not be used commercially. (See [usaspending.gov/db_info](https://www.usaspending.gov/db_info).) Post-2022 UEI-based records are free of this encumbrance.

---

## 9. Typical Users and Use Cases

- **Citizens and taxpayers** — seeing how tax dollars are spent (the FFATA raison d'être).
- **Journalists and watchdogs** — investigating waste, fraud, contractor concentration, and geographic distribution of federal money (e.g., COVID relief tracking).
- **Congress, GAO, Inspectors General** — oversight; GAO uses the data itself for subaward-quality audits.
- **Researchers and data scientists** — economics, political science, public administration studies of federal spending flows; the API and bulk files support large-scale analysis.
- **Businesses and contractors** — market research on who wins contracts, prime/sub relationships, competitive intelligence; small businesses identifying opportunities.
- **Grant recipients and state/local/tribal governments** — tracking awards to their jurisdictions, compliance with FFATA subaward reporting obligations (via FSRS/SAM.gov).
- **Federal agencies themselves** — Treasury returns standardized data back to agencies; agencies use submission statistics and Broker validation to manage their own reporting.

---

## 10. Benefits to the Public

1. **Transparency and accountability:** a single, free, searchable record of federal spending — a mandate from Congress aimed at curbing waste.
2. **"Follow the money" linkage:** the DATA Act's signature achievement — connecting appropriations to programs to awards to recipients and places, which was impossible before 2014.
3. **Standardization:** one data model (GSDM) across 100+ agencies, reducing reporting burden and enabling cross-agency comparison.
4. **Economic insight:** geographic (state, county, congressional district) breakdowns support local journalism, regional economic analysis, and community advocacy.
5. **Innovation substrate:** open API and full database downloads power third-party tools, academic research, and commercial analytics at no cost.
6. **Historical record:** the only longitudinal, transaction-level public record of federal awards (replacing discontinued Census reports), now spanning FY2001–present.

---

## 11. Practical Notes for Preservationists and Data Scientists

- **Snapshot discipline:** because agencies republish/recertify prior periods, a "FY2019 file" downloaded in 2020 may differ from one downloaded today. The Archive's **Full + Delta file scheme** is the sanctioned way to track revisions. The `Assistance_Delta`/`Contracts_Delta` files and the API's `/awards/last_updated/` endpoint help.
- **Persistent identifiers:** FAIN, PIID, URI, UEI, and TAS are the durable join keys; DUNS appears in legacy records.
- **Breaking changes to watch:** the DUNS→UEI transition (April 2022), DAIMS→GSDM (Nov. 2023), monthly vs. quarterly cadence (FY2022), and GAO-documented changes in reporting standards over time — all mean longitudinal analyses need version-aware methodology.
- **Recommended citation:** USAspending.gov provides a suggested format in the Analyst's Guide: *"USAspending.gov, U.S. Department of Treasury, Bureau of the Fiscal Service, https://www.usaspending.gov. Accessed [date]."*
- **Scale:** full PostgreSQL snapshot >1.5 TB; a single year of transaction data is very large — plan storage accordingly.
- **Always read the disclosures:** sitewide Award Data Disclosures, the Agency Submission Statistics page, and the Data Limitations documentation before publishing conclusions based on the data.

---

## Key Source Links

- About & legal authority: https://www.usaspending.gov/about
- Treasury reporting rules: https://tfx.treasury.gov/tfm/volume1/part2/chapter-6000-agency-reporting-requirements-usaspendinggov
- CRS overview: https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R44027
- Data documentation: https://www.usaspending.gov/data-sources ; https://www.usaspending.gov/federal-spending-guide
- API: https://api.usaspending.gov
- GAO audits: [GAO-18-138](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-18-138), [GAO-20-75](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-20-75), [GAO-22-104702](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-104702), [GAO-24-106237](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-24-106237.pdf)

**Bottom line:** USAspending.gov is a legally mandated, Treasury-published, open-data platform born from FFATA (2006), launched by OMB (2007), and transformed by the DATA Act (2014) into a standardized, machine-readable record of virtually all federal spending. It is uniquely valuable and freely reusable (with a minor legacy D&B caveat), but any rigorous use — especially historical or subaward-level analysis — must account for its well-documented data-quality limitations and retroactive revisions.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Let me dig deeper into USAspending-specific changes, the staffing tracker, and any policy proposals affecting the DATA Act.The staffing tracker's data loads via JavaScript, but I have good news coverage on Treasury staffing. Notably, I found that Congress *strengthened* the mandate in September 2026 (Stop Secret Spending Act). Now let me check the ICR status, recent GAO findings, and whether publications stayed on schedule.I now have GAO's 2026 testimony confirming ongoing data challenges. Let me check the Federal Register for recent notices and look for any specific impacts on the USAspending/Data Transparency team.I've reached the search limit, but I can still fetch pages directly. Let me verify the site's current status and check the Federal Register API for recent USAspending mentions.The Federal Register results show agencies continued citing USAspending data in rulemaking through September 2026, with no notices proposing its removal. The submission-statistics fetch failed with a proxy error, so I'll verify the site is live directly.I've now gathered sufficient evidence. One note on methodology: my direct fetches of usaspending.gov pages returned a proxy TLS error (HTTP 525), but numerous independent sources from 2026 — GAO testimony, Federal Register rules, and press analyses — confirm the site remains live and actively cited as the authoritative source, so this appears to be a fetch-tool artifact rather than a site outage. Here is the risk assessment.

---

# Risk Assessment: USAspending.gov

**Assessment date:** October 2026 (based on most recent available sources)

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence considered:**

- *No Known Issue level:* The "About the Data" documentation (last updated **November 19, 2025**) still describes the full historical span: award data from FY 2001, account data from FY 2017 Q2, all accessible via the Award Data Archive, Custom Downloads, and full database snapshots. No source found — GAO, press, or the site's own disclosures — reports any removal of prior-year files. ([About the Data PDF](https://www.usaspending.gov/data/about-the-data-download.pdf))
- *Mitigating factors:* Agencies routinely republish and recertify prior periods (standard practice, not removal); the DUNS-to-UEI identifier transition (April 2022) left legacy fields intact rather than deleting them. GAO's March 2026 testimony (GAO-26-109034) critiques data *quality and completeness*, not availability of history.
- *No evidence found* of removals comparable to the 2025 removals seen at other federal data sources (e.g., CDC pages). USAspending's FY 2001–FY 2025 award data remain referenced as available in 2026 GAO and Federal Register documents.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Historical files remain publicly available with no known alterations beyond routine, well-documented agency republishing.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence considered:**

- *No Known Issue level:* Monthly agency reporting (Files A/B/C, per OMB M-20-21) continued through FY 2025–2026. A GAO workforce report (GAO-26-108583, 2026) and Federal Register rulemakings (Dec 2025, April 2026, Sept 2026) all treat USAspending as a current, live source. Critically, **Congress enacted the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025 (P.L. 119-106, Sept. 11, 2026)**, which explicitly requires Treasury to continue and *expand* USAspending.gov publication — adding other transaction agreement (OTA) data within 3 years, an annual "unreported funding" report within 1 year, and an OTA compilation/plan if deadlines slip. ([Public Law 119-106](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ106/html/PLAW-119publ106.htm))
- *Risk factors:* Treasury/Bureau of the Fiscal Service workforce reductions (below) could strain operations; massive 2025 contract and grant terminations (USAID, DOGE actions) change the *content* of the data, though not its publication.
- *ICR status:* DATA Act/FFATA reporting is statutorily mandated; no evidence of an expired or lapsed information collection was found, and the reporting framework remains active in Treasury's Financial Manual and OMB guidance.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Publication continued on schedule through 2026, and the statutory mandate was just reinforced and expanded rather than weakened.

## Data Quality

**Evidence considered:**

- *Positive:* Reporting frequency *improved* over time (quarterly → monthly for all agencies in FY 2022); GAO-20-75 through GAO-22-104702 documented steady improvement in award-record consistency (from <1% fully consistent in 2017 to 84–96% for budgetary records by FY2018).
- *Moderate Risk level:* GAO's March 2026 testimony (**GAO-26-109034, "Federal Information Transparency: Action Needed"**) and April 2026 coverage document persistent gaps: ~$77.5 billion in DoD OTAs (FY2021–2025) reported in SAM.gov but *not* on USAspending; subaward completeness/accuracy problems; 49 of 152 agencies not reporting; data-quality gaps on emergency-supplemental awards. Separately, **GAO-25-107469** found only 51% of agencies completed required FPDS procurement data quality reports for FY2023, and 19 of 24 reviewed reports missed OMB deadlines — and FPDS feeds USAspending. (Sources: [GAO-26-109034](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-109034), [GAO-25-107469](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-25-107469.pdf), [Federal News Network, April 2026](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/agency-oversight/2026/04/federal-transparency-improved-on-paper-key-gaps-still-undermine-integrity-gao/))
- *Structural context:* These gaps are long-standing, not newly created since 2025. However, the ~11% governmentwide workforce decline in 2025 (GAO-26-108583) and the wave of contract/grant terminations create genuine emerging risk to upstream data quality from reporting agencies.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Granularity, timeliness, and frequency have been *maintained* (and frequency previously improved), which alone would indicate "No Known Issue." However, documented lapses in agency data-quality certification (over half of agencies noncompliant for FY2023), persistent OTA/subaward gaps spanning current years, and severe staffing losses at reporting agencies constitute a real, emerging risk to quality rather than a hypothetical one.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence considered:**

- *No Known Issue level:* USAspending.gov is among the most explicitly mandated federal datasets in existence: **FFATA (2006)** created the website by name in statute (single free public searchable website); the **DATA Act (2014)** transferred it to Treasury and expanded required content; the **CBJTA (2021)** added budget-justification linkage; and the **Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025 (P.L. 119-106, Sept. 2026)** just strengthened it again — the statute literally defines "USAspending.gov" as a term and imposes new reporting duties on the Treasury Secretary. Treasury's Financial Manual (TFM Vol. I, Pt. 2, Ch. 6000) identifies FFATA as amended as the primary authority, and 31 U.S.C. § 6101 note codifies the requirements. It is required for implementation of a federal program (governmentwide spending transparency), has immense programmatic use (Congress, GAO, agencies, Federal Register rulemakings all rely on it), and has no full substitute — FPDS, SAM.gov, and GTAS are partial upstream feeds that USAspending uniquely unifies.
- *High Risk considerations:* None apply — authorization is explicit, not vague; no alternative collection can substitute.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** The clearest possible statutory footing, recently reaffirmed and expanded by Congress with bipartisan support (the Senate companion was S.872; the House bill H.R. 2069).

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence considered:**

- *High Risk level evidence:* Treasury Department lost **31,600+ employees (~28%) in 2025** ([Federal News Network, Jan. 2026](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce/2026/01/how-staffing-cuts-in-2025-transformed-the-federal-workforce/)) — far above the 1,000-employee threshold — though cuts were concentrated in the IRS. GAO (GAO-26-108583) found all 22 CFO Act agencies lost staff in 2025.
- *Moderate Risk level evidence:* The **Bureau of the Fiscal Service itself** — the operating bureau for USAspending — was directed under the "Optimizing the Federal Workforce" Executive Order to reduce its workforce; union officials expected **up to 25% of the bureau's ~3,300 employees to be cut**, with RIFs, outsourced offices (savings bonds servicing, check printing), and ~80 probationary employees laid off in Parkersburg in Feb. 2025 (later reinstated under court order). ([GovExec, April 2025](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/04/treasury-eliminates-offices-and-outsources-work-more-layoffs-coming/404472/)) Treasury's FY2026 budget in brief cites $47.5M in savings from the BFS appropriation. ([Treasury FY2026 BIB](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/266/12.-Fiscal-FY-2026-BIB.pdf))
- *Countervailing:* The announced cuts targeted paper-based operations (bond servicing, check printing), not the Data Transparency function; the FY2025 budget in brief explicitly funded a Data Strategy initiative to *improve* USAspending.gov. The site continued operating and publishing through 2026, and Congress simultaneously imposed *new* obligations (Stop Secret Spending Act) presupposing a functioning team.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** At the bureau level (the unit that actually operates USAspending), documented losses of roughly 25% of staff and mandated RIFs fall squarely in the 10–39% band. Department-wide Treasury losses (~28%, >31,000) would technically trigger the "1,000 or more staff lost" High-Risk threshold, but those cuts were concentrated in the IRS rather than the Fiscal Service transparency function — and the platform's continued operation and statutory expansion suggest the core function has so far been preserved. This is the category with the most genuine uncertainty.

## Policy

**Evidence considered:**

- *No Known Issue level:* No presidential action, executive order, or OMB directive since January 2025 reduces what USAspending collects or publishes. A Federal Register search shows agencies (SEC, Commerce, DOL) *continued citing USAspending data* in rulemaking through September 2026, treating it as the authoritative source. GAO's 2026 oversight attention pushes toward *more* transparency, not less. Notably, the platform's mission aligns with the administration's stated waste-cutting agenda — DOGE itself relied on (and was fact-checked against) FPDS/USAspending data ([NPR, Feb. 2025](https://www-s1.npr.org/2025/02/19/nx-s1-5302705/doge-overstates-savings-federal-contracts)), and GAO's harshest 2025–2026 transparency criticism targeted DOGE's own opaque "Wall of Receipts" (GAO-26-108615), not USAspending.
- *Moderate Risk considerations:* The broader 2025–2026 environment included removals of other federal datasets and deregulatory initiatives (e.g., rescission of contractor-related rules citing USAspending data), which created general pressure on federal data infrastructure. But no administration statement or action specifically targeting USAspending was found.
- *Positive policy signals:* The Stop Secret Spending Act (enacted Sept. 11, 2026) is a direct congressional endorsement of the platform's continuation and expansion.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what USAspending collects and publishes; policy momentum (statutory expansion, GAO oversight, continued regulatory reliance) points toward continuity.

## Overall Assessment

USAspending.gov is among the **lowest-risk federal datasets** for removal or loss of access. Its statutory mandate is explicit, recently reaffirmed (P.L. 119-106, Sept. 2026), and the platform continued publishing on schedule through 2026 while other federal data sources faced disruption. The two genuine areas of concern are **(1) upstream data quality** — long-standing OTA and subaward gaps compounded by lapses in agency data-quality certification and an 11% governmentwide workforce decline — and **(2) the uncertain depth of Bureau of the Fiscal Service staffing cuts** (up to ~25% of the bureau), which could erode the team's capacity to meet its existing and newly expanded obligations. Preservationists should note that while removal risk is low, **retroactive restatement of prior-period data is routine**, so regular snapshot archiving remains worthwhile; data scientists should treat pre-FY2017 data and subaward records with the documented quality caveats from GAO's 2024–2026 findings.

**Caveats:** My direct verification of the live site was impeded by a fetch-proxy TLS error, and the USAJobs staffing tracker (which ceased collection Dec. 31, 2025) could not provide bureau-specific numbers; staffing findings rely on 2025 press reporting and GAO workforce data, and the final Fiscal Service RIF numbers may differ from early projections.
